{{right|''Kingsley'', Yeast, vii. (Da}}}}

¶
'''tostication''' (tos-ti-kā′shon), ''n.'' [< ''tosticat''(''ed'') + ''-ion''.] The state of being tossed about; commotion; disturbance; perplexity. [Prov. Eng.]

{{smaller block|After all, methinks, I want those ''tostications'' (thou seest how women, and women's words, fill my mind) to be over happily over, that I may sit down quietly and reflect.
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, III. lxviii.}}}}

'''tosunder†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''tosondren''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''sunder''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] To go to pieces; split.

{{smaller block|The fyry welkne gan to thundir,
As thou the world schulde alle ''tosondre''.
{{right|''Gower'', MS. Soc. Antiq. 134, f. 91. (''Halliwell''.)}}}}

'''toswap†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''toswappen''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''swap''.] To smite heavily.

{{smaller block|So fuersly in fight fellis oure knightes,
Al''to swappon'' vs with swerdes & with swym strokes.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 9561.}}}}

'''toswink†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''toswinken''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''swink''.] To toil excessively; labor hard.

{{smaller block|In erthe, in eir, in water men ''to-swinke''
To gete a glotoun deyntee mete and drinke.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Pardoner's Tale, l. 57.}}}}

'''tosy''' (tō′zi), ''a.'' [< ''tose'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Teased, as wool; hence, woolly; soft. Also ''tozy''. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''tot<sup>1</sup>''' (tot), ''n.'' [< Icel. ''tottr'' = Dan. ''tot'', a nickname of a dwarf. Cf. ''tit''<sup>3</sup>.] 1. Anything small or insignificant; especially, a small child: used as a term of endearment.

{{smaller block|Now, Jenny! can there greater pleasure be
Than see sic wee ''tots'' toolying at your knee?
{{right|''Ramsay'', Gentle Shepherd (Works, II. 81).}}}}

¶
2. A drinking-cup holding about half a pint; also, a small quantity; especially, when applied to liquor, as much as makes a draught or dram. [Prov. Eng.]

{{smaller block|He had no society of any kind, and often found himself pining for . . . the glare of the camp-fires, the fragrant fumes of the "honey dew," and the ''tot'' of rum that passed from beard to beard.
{{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, II. i.}}}}

3. A foolish fellow. [Prov. Eng.]

'''tot<sup>2</sup>''' (tot), ''n.'' [< L. ''tot'', so much, so many; by some explained as an abbr. of L. ''totus'', or E. ''total'', all. Cf. ''tot<sup>2</sup>'', ''v.'', ''tote<sup>3</sup>'', ''v.''] 1. Originally, so many; so much: formerly written opposite an item in an account to indicate that the debt was good. The full expression is given as ''tot pecuniæ regi debetur'', so much money is due to the king.

{{smaller block|Totted, A Term us'd in the Exchequer, when the foreign Opposer, or other Officer, has noted a good Debt to the Queen as such, by writing the word ''Tot'' to it.
{{right|''E. Phillips'', World of Words, 1706.}}}}

2. An exercise in addition; a sum. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|Graduated Exercises in Addition (''Tots'' and Cross ''Tots'', Simple and Compound).
{{right|''Athenæum'', No. 3268, p. 757.}}}}

'''tot<sup>2</sup>''' (tot), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''totted'', ppr. ''totting''. [ME. ''totten''; < ''tot<sup>2</sup>'', ''n.'' Cf. ''tote<sup>3</sup>''.] 1. To mark (an account or a name) with the word ''tot'': as, to ''tot'' an item in a bill. See ''tot<sup>2</sup>'', ''n.'', 1.

{{smaller block|Sir, ther arn xv. jurores abowe to certifie ye, as many as ye will; but lete these men that be ''tottid'' be certified, for thei be the rewleris.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 55.}}}}

2. To count up; add; sum: usually with ''up''. [Colloq.]

¶
'''tota''' (tō′tä), ''n.'' [Native name.] A monkey: same as ''grivet.''

'''total''' (tō′tal), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''totall'', < OF. (and F.) ''total'' = Sp. Pg. ''total'' = It. ''totale'' = G. ''total'', < ML. ''totalis'', entire, total (''summa totalis'', the sum total, the whole amount), < L. ''totus'', whole, entire.] '''I.''' ''a.'' 1. Pertaining to or constituting a whole or the whole; being or taken together; undivided.

{{smaller block|So many there are of them in the Citadell that I think the ''totall'' number of them is at the least two hundred.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 125.}}}}

{{smaller block|As the ''total'' tonnage [of Venetian merchant vessels] is but 26,000, it may be inferred that they are small craft.
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xvi.}}}}

2. Comprising the whole; lacking no member or part; complete; entire.

{{smaller block|One Day Jove
Sent Hermes down to Ida's Grove,
Commanding Cupid to deliver
His Store of Darts, his ''total'' Quiver.
{{right|''Prior'', Mercury and Cupid.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''total'' grist unsifted, husks and all.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, vi. 108.}}}}

{{smaller block|Then we dipt in all
That treats of whatsoever is, the state,
The ''total'' chronicles of man.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, ii.}}}}

3. Complete in degree; absolute; unqualified; utter: as, a ''total'' change; ''total'' darkness.

{{smaller block|O dark, dark, dark, amid the blaze of noon,
Irrecoverably dark, ''total'' eclipse
Without all hope of day! ''Milton'', S. A., l. 81.}}
